The eleven ratings for MITIE

MITIE Group PLC (MTO-GB): no longer an equity thesis, but a fairly priced 4.3% cash spread with a one-in-ten chance of a 20% to 25% fall

Investment memo for Richard, written 25-Oct-2026. Share price 210.8p (21-Oct-2026). Recommended cash offer from OCS Group (owned by the private-equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, "CD&R") at 218.5p, plus a 1.3p interim dividend if the scheme is not effective by 19-Nov-2026. Market value about £2.9bn; fiscal year to 31 March. The bases of the figures are set out in the end notes.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one sentence. Mitie is no longer an equity thesis: Mitie's shares are now a 4.3% cash spread with roughly a one-in-ten chance of becoming an equity thesis again at a 20% to 25% lower price, and the market has priced that one-in-ten chance fairly.

The eight things that matter

  1. The merger spread is fairly priced, so there is no edge on either side. The Analyst's own estimate of the break probability (9% to 11%) sits inside the 9% to 12% that the price implies. The 1.3p interim dividend belongs in the expected receipt because completion is expected in calendar Q1 2027, after the 19-Nov-2026 cut-off that triggers the dividend. The spread therefore pays about the risk-free rate for bearing a one-in-ten chance of a 20% to 25% loss: the correct price for the risk, not a bargain.
  2. Only one regulator, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), stands between the holder and the cash. The CMA ran its invitation to comment from 15 to 29-Sep-2026 but, as of 22-Oct-2026, had not launched Phase 1, so its 40-working-day clock had not started. OCS may seek to lapse the offer on a Phase 2 reference or on remedies "adverse to a material extent", and there is no break fee. Three facts point to clearance: the Interserve precedent (Phase 1 clearance in seven weeks, 2020), a combined UK facilities share below 20% (about 16% of security and 12% of cleaning), and committed financing. The risks are overlap in public-sector work and objections from rivals who argue that the combination removes one of only two or three national bidders for integrated contracts.
  3. The standalone business is better than its reputation and its forecasts are unusually predictable, but a listed holder benefits from those forecasts only if the deal breaks. Two analysts working in sequence, three brokers and the model all land on FY27 EBIT of £300m to £306m (a margin of 5.0% to 5.1%), because the year's change consists of a handful of disclosed, dated and mostly contracted items. The resulting FY27 range of outcomes, about minus 4% to plus 3% on EBIT, is narrow for this sector.
  4. The FY27 margin step is a release of existing self-help, not a new capability. The margin stayed flat at 4.6% to 4.7% for three years because each year's £20m to £25m of self-help was spent absorbing a statutory cost shock (National Living Wage +9.8% in April 2024; +6.7% plus higher employer National Insurance in April 2025). FY27 is the first year since FY24 with no new shock, so the same self-help reaches the margin, with Marlowe synergies and the drop-out of a telecoms contract loss on top. The corollary is that every FY28 margin forecast is, in effect, a forecast of the Autumn Budget of 28-Oct-2026 and of the April 2027 wage floor.
  5. The consensus EPS growth headline of "+15%" for FY27 flatters, because it compares two different share counts. Consensus compares a diluted FY26 base (12.6p) with a post-dilution FY27 share count. On the company's basic basis the growth is +7% (Jefferies) to +12% (the model: 13.6p to 15.2p). About 80m nil-cost options vested and were exercised between March and October 2026, lifting voting rights from 1,255m to 1,301.7m despite buybacks; that 6% to 7% dilution is already in the share count but absent from the growth narrative.
  6. Earnings quality is the weakest foundation of the case; cash quality is better than feared. Other items (costs excluded from adjusted profit) were £113m in FY26, 43% of EBIT, so reported basic EPS of 6.6p was barely half of adjusted EPS of 13.6p: a 106% gap, against a 20% to 30% peer median. About £25m a year of restructuring is recurring in substance (Mitie has run a named programme every year since 2017), so "clean" EPS runs about 1.5p a year below adjusted EPS. On the cash side, FY26 free cash flow of £162m was earned despite a £35.7m working-capital outflow (not helped by an inflow, as one earlier set of numbers assumed), invoice discounting was closed in FY23, and leverage is 1.1x to 1.2x, with covenant leverage of 0.82x against a 3.0x limit.
  7. The business has a structural margin ceiling, and its owners sold at that ceiling. Mitie's prices are cost pass-through (94% of wage inflation and 76% of statutory costs recovered), clients claim most automation savings at once or at re-tender, and the UK state (45% to 50% of revenue) is turning toward insourcing through a Public Interest Test from April 2027. The plausible margin ceiling is about 5.5% by FY30. The offer, at 12x two-year-forward earnings, sits at the 95th percentile of Mitie's own ten-year range and about 35% above a standalone fair value of 160p to 175p: full by Mitie's history, but only fair by private-market precedent (about 8.5x EBITDA, against the 12x paid for unlisted business-services companies since 2020). A counter-bid is possible in theory and unlikely in practice.
  8. In a break, the order of events would matter more than the forecasts. Merger-arbitrage holders would sell first into a thin UK mid-cap market, taking the price toward 150p to 165p (LMR Partners and others have been buying from long-only sellers, and Oasis's undertakings over its 9.9% swap position lapse with the scheme). Consensus would then cut FY28 by 3% to 6% (share count, leadership transition, no buyback assumed). Only after that would the £81m remaining buyback restart and a successor chief executive be named, and the stock would re-rate toward 9.5x to 10x only on a clean FY27 print. That sequence is the only route by which Richard's framework could apply to Mitie: a break-day price of 150p to 165p against a guideline-multiple value of about 189p at September 2027 would be a "cause for concern clearing" setup in a medium-quality, low-cyclicality business.

Implications for Richard

As a holder

Hold for the spread only if content to carry a one-in-ten chance of a 20% to 25% loss for an expected return of about the risk-free rate. Selling at 210.8p gives up 9p of likely cash in exchange for certainty, a reasonable trade only if the capital has a better use.

As a non-holder

Do nothing before the CMA decides, but set an alert for a Phase 2 reference or a lapse. A break-day price below 160p would justify a fresh look as a reversion case, with the caveats set out in #9 and #10: leadership in transition, consensus cutting first, and a market regime that refuses re-ratings to UK mid-caps.

The one event that moves the price

The CMA decision, expected between late 2026 and early 2027, is the only dated event that changes the share price. The Budget and the H1 results matter only to the standalone case that a break would expose.

The five judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic

Five judgements drive the value of the shares over the next one to two years. The CMA judgement dwarfs the other four while the offer stands; the other four become live only in a break.

5. Break-case multiple 9.5x to 10x, buyback restartsGuideline 9.52xEach turn of P/E is about 17.5p (10%); buyback worth 2% to 4% of EPS by FY299x gives about 158p; 10.5x about 184p

Judgement 1: why the spread is fairly priced. The break value is brokers'-basis 24-month-forward EPS of about 17.0p to 17.5p (with no buyback) at 9.5x to 10x, which gives 162p to 175p. On the day of a break, arbitrage selling would likely overshoot toward the undisturbed price of 151p (Direct Line fell 16% on the day Ageas walked away). The loss is 17% to 24% from 210.8p, or 20% to 27% against the 219.8p a holder expected. Weighted by a 10% probability, the expected cost of a break is about 5p to 6p, or 2.5% of the price, almost exactly what the 4.3% spread pays above the risk-free rate. That match between the expected cost and the excess return is why the spread is fairly priced.

Judgement 2: a 50 basis point FY27 margin miss is possible, but would need four things to go wrong together. A 50 basis point miss on £6,000m of revenue is £30m of EBIT, £22.5m of attributable profit after 25% tax and 1.75p of EPS over 1,285m shares. The realistic FY27 range is nearer plus or minus 20 basis points (plus or minus £12m of EBIT; plus or minus 0.7p of EPS). The full 50 basis points would need four adverse outcomes at once: the inflation recovery rate falling from 93% to 88% (£7m), Technical Services staying at minus 3% for the year (£6m), Marlowe churn (£5m) and synergy slippage (£5m).

Judgement 3: a Budget shock would cost £12m to £15m of FY28 EBIT; a benign surprise would add only £5m to £10m. A repeat of the FY26 employer National Insurance step (gross £48.5m, 76% recovered) would leave £10m to £12m unrecovered in the year it arrives. A 5.5% wage floor instead of 3.7% would add about £35m of gross cost on the roughly £2bn of wages near the floor, of which about 6% (£2m) plus the indexation lag would go unrecovered. Together those two shocks cost £12m to £15m, 20 basis points of FY28 margin and 0.7p to 0.9p of EPS. In the reverse case, an employer National Insurance holiday for workers aged 20 to 24 (floated in Deutsche Bank's preview) would save perhaps £20m to £35m gross on the Analyst's arithmetic, but clients would claim most of that saving under the same change-of-law clauses, leaving perhaps £5m to £10m with Mitie.

Judgement 4: Marlowe churn is costly because Marlowe's costs are fixed. Marlowe's drop-through on lost revenue is about 25% (Deutsche Bank's estimate), far above the group's 7% to 10%, because its field force is a fixed route network: losing 10% of about £400m of compliance revenue (£40m) costs about £10m of profit. Marlowe's own acquisition history shows attrition spiking to about 20% after a deal and settling below 10% within two years, so some churn is normal, and the base case already carries a £5m dis-synergy line. Synergies of £20m rather than £25m in FY28 would cost another £5m, for a total of £15m, or 0.9p of EPS.

Judgement 5: the sector sets about two-thirds of the break-case multiple. The sector sets about two-thirds of the multiple (ISS trades at 11.8x and Serco at 11.7x; Mitie's pre-bid beta to the sector was about 0.8), and Mitie's own issues set the other third (succession, UK public exposure, the gap between adjusted and statutory earnings, and the arbitrage overhang). Each turn of P/E on 17.5p of EPS is worth 17.5p of value. A full £100m buyback a year adds about 5% to EPS (Jefferies); the model's £50m to £75m a year from FY28 adds 2% to 4% by FY29.

Scorecard: the twelve topics

#1Operating environment: a moderate near-term tailwind, a slow political headwind later

Judgement. Over the next six to twelve months Mitie's operating environment is a moderate net tailwind: the statutory cost shock is fading, demand indicators are at records, and the sector's dominant theme (private bids for cheap listed outsourcers) has already paid Mitie a 47% premium. Over 2027 to 2030, a slow political headwind (the insourcing of UK public work) and a structural margin cap offset much of that tailwind. The environment supports steady low-single-digit volume growth and a stable-to-slightly-rising margin; it does not support a re-rating story.

Evidence and inference

  • Costs: the inflation hurdle is falling, so more of Mitie's organic growth is now volume. The gross inflation hurdle falls from £170m in FY26 (£18.6m of it unrecovered before savings) to about £135m in FY27, with a guided net drag of £10m to £12m. The National Living Wage rose 4.1% in April 2026, against 6.7% a year earlier, and private-sector wage growth is slowing toward 3%. The price element of organic growth therefore falls from about 3 points in FY26 to about 2 in FY27, so a steady 4% organic growth rate now contains more volume than it did.
  • Structural demand drivers give multi-year visibility. The drivers are regulation, decarbonisation, water investment, data centres and public capital programmes:
    Regulation Building Safety Act; Martyn's Law (venue terrorism-preparedness duties); fire and water compliance Decarbonisation Energy Performance Certificate rating B required by 2030 for let commercial buildings; a £1.1bn UK commercial heat market growing about 30% a year Water the industry's eighth five-year investment period (AMP8), £104bn to 2030 Data centres Public capital programmes prisons, NHS, education, defence
  • Competitive intensity is easing at the top of the market and intensifying at its edges. Sodexo, ISS and Capita have all turned margin-first, and Capita has withdrawn from central government bidding. At the edges, mid-market low bidders cost Mitie about 30 basis points on contested public renewals, and private-equity-backed compliance platforms contest Marlowe's small clients. The OCS combination itself removes a top-five rival.
The largest structural threat: insourcing of UK public work, biting from FY29. From 1-Apr-2027 a Public Interest Test requires central government contracts above £1m (cleaning and security are named first) to be assessed for insourcing before re-tender. An Insourcing Unit launched on 29-Sep-2026, Transport for London is piloting insourced cleaning, and the Two-Tier Workforce Code returns from October 2026. With 45% to 50% of Mitie's revenue public, the Test is the largest structural threat to the business, but the Test works through renewals of 5-to-10-year contracts, so it bites from FY29. Defence, justice and vetted secure sites (Landmarc, the Atomic Weapons Establishment, immigration) are largely exempt or impractical to insource, which leaves perhaps £800m to £1bn of the book exposed.
So what. The near-term environment makes the FY27 margin floor easy to clear and the FY28 margin step plausible; the medium-term environment caps the standalone case at about 4% organic growth and a 5.5% margin. For a listed holder, the bid has already monetised the environmental tailwind.

Counter-case

Automation is deflationary for work billed by the hour: Securitas cites remote guarding cutting client budgets by up to 80% against manned guarding. Professional-services multiples are held down by the fear that artificial intelligence replaces labour. And the Budget could re-impose a statutory cost shock within days.

What would change the view

Worse: a Budget with a new employer cost step; a Cabinet Office insourcing roadmap naming cleaning and security contracts for 2027 to 2028. Better: evidence that the compliance cross-sell pipeline (about £700m of annual contract value) is converting into organic growth in compliance revenue.

Versus the market

The market agrees on the demand picture and mostly ignores the environment because the price is pinned to the offer. The Analyst differs in one emphasis: nobody frames the Budget of 28-Oct-2026 as the pivot for the FY28 margin, which it is.

Score: 55. A fading cost shock and record demand indicators make the near term supportive, but a slow political headwind on half the revenue base and a sector that caps margins near 5% keep Mitie in the middle of the European pack.

#2Internally-driven corporate change forces

Judgement. Mitie is undergoing strong, well-resourced internal change, and its owners have chosen to sell it. The standalone changes are real and mostly mechanical for the next 18 months. Their weakness is that they have not yet shown up in the margin or in clean earnings, and their decisive expression was a cash exit at 15x FY27 earnings rather than a chief executive succession.

Key point. The Marlowe synergy increments are the most reliable items in the forecast, and about a quarter of revenue now sits in compliance and projects lines with structurally higher margins than the 4% core; the leadership that built both leaves on completion.

Evidence and inference

The changes under way

  • The value-chain pivot from "facilities management" to "facilities transformation". The Marlowe acquisition (about £366m, August 2025) made Mitie the UK leader in facilities compliance: fire, water, air and building safety work that is non-discretionary and regulation-driven, earning 30% to 45% gross margins at private specialists against Mitie's 10.8% group gross margin. Facilities Compliance revenue was £421m in FY26 and £127m in Q1 FY27 (+144%). The projects ambition (decarbonisation, data centres, water) was raised to £2bn from £1.5bn, at margins above 9%, and the compliance ambition to £1.5bn. About a quarter of revenue is therefore now in lines with structurally higher margins than the 4% core.
  • The Marlowe integration is ahead of plan. Cost synergies were £7m in FY26 against about £5m expected, with £15m run-rate targeted for FY27 and £30m for FY28 (£16.5m of it from support functions; 15 properties exited; Salford Quays closing by December 2026; 25 acquired entities already on the IBM Maximo maintenance system).
  • Cost discipline and technology. Margin-enhancement savings of £25m in FY26 were fully retained but fully consumed by unrecovered statutory costs. The Target Operating Model programme (£70.7m cumulative cost) ends in March 2027, removing about £15m a year of cash cost below the adjusted line. Project PRIO, Mitie's agentic artificial intelligence programme, has about 70 live agents and £20m to £25m of FY27 cost below the adjusted line, but no disclosed savings target. Mitie runs over 1,000 cleaning robots, and its Aria app handles about 40% of service requests without human intervention.
  • Commercial recovery. Renewals rose from 59% to 91%, and the customer Net Promoter Score rose to +64 from +39 (FY22). Technical Services, under Sam White (from Costain, December 2025), had secured 70% of its FY27 sales target by Q1, 150% more than a year earlier, after a 5% revenue decline in Q1.
  • Capital allocation. Mitie has bought back £303m of shares since FY23 at 150p to 166p, accretive against the 218.5p offer. A new £100m programme launched in October 2025 was £81m complete by July 2026 and was suspended on the offer.

What holds the changes back, and who leaves

  • The negatives. Other items rose from £73m to £113m. Working capital drifted (FactSet net working capital moved from minus £102m at H2 FY24 to minus £19m at H2 FY26; debtor days from 29 to 31). Public contracts suffered execution failures: the Independent Monitoring Board found His Majesty's Prison Millsike "unsafe, understaffed" in September 2026, and one in five NHS cleaners' payslips were wrong, leading to strikes. Employee engagement is 63% against a 75% benchmark, and about 300 Marlowe staff left in Q1 FY27.
  • The change of control. Phil Bentley (chief executive since 2016, holding over 18m shares) and Simon Kirkpatrick (finance director) leave on completion, and OCS's Rob Legge and Gary McGaghey take over. Oasis (9.9% via a swap) and the directors (1.53%) gave irrevocable undertakings. Bentley's retirement had already been announced for spring 2027, with no successor named.
So what. The standalone changes justify the margin path from 4.7% to 5.05% to 5.3%, and little more; the sale converts those changes into a fixed 218.5p. In a break the changes would continue, but under a chief executive who is leaving and a finance director whose departure was tied to completion.

Counter-case

Jefferies' June 2025 downgrade argued that Marlowe moved Mitie away from disciplined organic delivery toward a "riskier roll-up conglomerate". Return on invested capital fell from 24.5% to 18.1%, and the Analyst estimates Marlowe's post-tax return at only 10% to 12% by FY28, even with full synergies.

What would change the view

Better: a disclosed PRIO savings figure at the H1 results; a named internal successor (for the break case). Worse: Marlowe revenue attrition beyond the competitor withdrawals already noted, since each £35m of lost Marlowe revenue costs about £9m of profit.

Versus the market

The sell-side knows the synergy phasing and the Interserve precedent well. It does not model Marlowe churn, includes no PRIO benefit, and does not frame the leadership position in a break as a succession already in progress (Bentley stays until a successor is found) rather than a vacancy. The Analyst is slightly more positive than the earlier analysis on the break-case leadership risk and slightly more negative on earnings quality.

Score: 58. A genuine, funded pivot into higher-margin compliance and projects, an integration running ahead of plan and a demonstrable commercial recovery, held back by recurring restructuring costs, frontline execution lapses and a leadership team that leaves with the deal.

#3Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Judgement. Mitie leads a moderately supportive but structurally low-margin industry, with a narrow moat that protects its right to win and keep work but not its prices. Its financial profile is asset-light and cash-generative, with an unclean earnings base. Its management is the strongest foundation of the standalone case, and that management is leaving. Net: a medium-quality business, run very well, that a bidder has priced as if it were a shade better.

Industry structure: Mitie leads a fragmented, contract-bound industry whose structure caps margins at 1% to 5%. Mitie is number one in UK facilities management with about a 14% share, twice the next competitor's, in an implied market of about £40bn. The top five firms plausibly hold 35% to 40% of the national market, above a fragmented local base that includes over 2,000 compliance firms. Contracts are long (5 to 10 years in the public sector, 3 to 5 in the private sector), about 90% indexed to inflation, dispersed across 3,000 clients with none above 10% of revenue, and protected by procurement barriers (1,100-page central government contracts; security vetting). The same structure caps margins on core cost-plus contracts at 1% to 5%, because clients claim savings and local firms cap prices. The industry's fragility is concentrated in one actor, the UK state, which is both its largest client and its regulator.

Business model and moat: the moat protects renewals, not prices. Mitie's four moderate advantages (scale, switching costs in integrated contracts, route density and vetting, and regulatory access) together produce 91% renewals and a record order book. They do not produce pricing power: the margin stayed flat at 4.6% to 4.7% for three years despite full cost pass-through. Because integrated services reach only 40% of the largest customers, Mitie has room to deepen those relationships. The moat is widening in technical and compliance work and narrowing in public soft services.

Financial profile: Mitie earns high returns on little capital, on a thin margin and an unclean earnings base.

Strengths

  • Return on invested capital 18.1% (24.5% before Marlowe; target above 20%), against 9% to 11% at ISS and 7% at Sodexo
  • Capital spending about 0.7% of revenue; FY26 free cash flow of £162m, about 100% of adjusted attributable profit
  • Net debt including leases £444m (1.37x on FactSet's definition; 1.2x average; covenant leverage 0.82x); interest cover about 9x
  • £360m of fixed-rate US private placement notes at 4.65% to 2034 and an undrawn £250m facility to October 2028

Weaknesses

  • An operating margin of 4.7%, in the lower half of peers (Serco about 6%, ISS 5.0% to 5.25%, Securitas 8%, Compass 7.4%)
  • A 106% gap between adjusted and basic EPS
  • Shareholders' equity of only about £438m and negative tangible equity, because the assets are goodwill and intangibles
  • EPS on the brokers' basis grew only 4% and 7% in FY25 and FY26, while revenue grew 14% and 11%

Management: an excellent record of action, a modern board, and one blind spot, succession.

The record

Bentley led a turnaround from the 2016-2017 accounting crisis (net assets cut by £272m to £90m), integrated Interserve at 1.8 times the synergy target, and lifted the margin from 2.3% (FY21) to 4.7% (FY24). Management met every target of the FY22-FY24 plan, met the FY25-FY27 revenue target a year early, earned seven consecutive consensus profit upgrades after the October 2023 capital markets event, beat FY26 free cash flow guidance by 35%, bought back shares at low multiples and exited at a 47% premium.

Governance and culture

Governance is modern: seven of nine directors are independent, malus and clawback apply, a 7.5% negative discretion was applied to a vested award, and management asked for the FY26 bonus to be cut. Pay has two blemishes: a one-off award of 600% of salary to defer retirement, and retention bonuses of 150% of salary on completion. The culture is cost-led and commercial at the top and thin at the frontline.

The blind spot

Succession. No internal successor emerged, the board hired the search firm Egon Zehnder, and the board then chose a sale.

Counter-case

The most advantaged businesses in this sector are specialists and caterers, not generalists. Mitie's compliance pivot is early and its discipline in rolling up acquisitions is unproven. A lean organisation that fails a prison mobilisation and a payroll does not have a "winning culture" in the total-system sense.

What would change the view

Better: disclosed Facilities Compliance margins converging toward private specialists' 8% to 10%. Worse: a second serious failure in mobilising a public contract. Either way: the identity of the successor in a break.

Versus the market

Consensus and the Analyst agree on the industry structure. The market's narrative under-weights two things: that the moat protects renewals rather than prices, which is why scale never reached the margin; and that management quality is a standalone asset that the buyer, not the listed holder, now owns.

Score: 55. A clear market leader with high returns on a small capital base and a very good management record, in an industry whose contract structure fixes margins near 5%, with an earnings base that is among the least clean in the sector and a leadership team that leaves on completion.

#4Conservative guidance, expectations management and the record of delivery

Judgement. Mitie's guidance is a floor, set by a management that has cleared every floor since 2023; consensus sits exactly on that floor, and the Takeover Code locks the floor until completion. The gap between the Analyst's expectation and the guidance is favourable but small (about £4m of EBIT) and, if the deal completes, the gap accrues to CD&R. Mitie earns a high mark for its guidance behaviour and a low one for that behaviour's usefulness to a listed holder now.

Evidence and inference

  • The FY27 targets are now formal profit forecasts, so a change to them is costly. On 21-Jul-2026 the company confirmed that the FY27 targets are profit forecasts under Rule 28.1 of the Takeover Code, so any change needs reports from reporting accountants and financial advisers. At the H1 results on 19-Nov-2026, the Analyst puts the probabilities at about 88% reiterated, 7% reduced (a de facto profit warning) and 5% raised in form; good news would arrive as "ahead of expectations" wording, not as a new number.

  • Consensus is drifting up with the margin step already embedded, so there is no low base from which to be surprised. Three brokers cover the stock (Jefferies, Deutsche Bank and Investec), all with Hold ratings and target prices of 219p to 221p; none rates it a Buy. Consensus FY27 EBIT is £301m (5.0%) and free cash flow £150m. Over one, three and six months, EPS estimates rose 1% to 2%, EBITDA estimates 0% to 1%, and the target price 3%, 8% and 10% (toward the offer).

The record: Mitie is a precise sandbagger on profit and cash, and an honest tracker on revenue. Management cleared every profit and cash floor it set since 2023; its only misses were revenue and interest. The headline margin target was never raised in three years; management raised adjacent ambitions (projects, compliance, the savings target) instead.

Informal commentary at the annual general meeting of 21-Jul-2026, held on bid day and so with every incentive to show standalone strength, expressed "absolute confidence" in the targets and highlighted Technical Services' secured sales and a ten-fold rise in the compliance cross-sell pipeline.

The FY27 floor is attainable with modest headroom, not deeply sandbagged. The Analyst's indicative bridge takes FY26 EBIT of £264m to about £304m (5.05%), only about £4m above the 5% floor, because the lost DWP contract and continuing net inflation absorb most of the gains from synergies and the telecoms drop-out.

So what. Mitie will very probably meet or slightly beat its FY27 profit guidance: the Analyst puts "met or beaten on margin" at about 85%, and "met or beaten on cash" at about 70%, depending on whether the £150m is stated before or after OCS transaction costs. None of that outcome moves the share price while the offer stands.

Counter-case

Mitie's record of beating floors coexists with a record of the margin not moving for three years: a margin step is new ground even though each component is old ground. The free cash flow floor is also the less certain of the two, because FY27 carries about £60m of cash other items (Target Operating Model about £15m, PRIO about £22m, Marlowe integration about £10m, OCS transaction costs about £13m) and about £20m to £25m of working capital for projects.

What would change the view

An H1 margin below 4.3% or above 4.8% (the Analyst's base is about 4.5%, against about 4.3% a year earlier); a qualification of the £150m cash guidance; management attaching a number to PRIO savings.

Versus the market

The Analyst agrees with the market on the headline but differs on the share count. Consensus FY27 EPS of 14.5p uses a diluted count of about 1,310m to 1,340m shares, so its "+15%" growth is +7% to +12% on the company's basic basis. Deutsche Bank's standalone count (1,255m, unchanged after the buyback suspension) overstates its standalone EPS by 3% to 4%, an error that would be corrected the day a lapse was announced. In a break, the first consensus move would be down, not up.

Score: 62. A textbook floor-setter with a clean three-year record of clearing floors and raising ambitions quietly, marked down because the floor is locked by the Takeover Code, consensus already sits on it and any beat belongs to the acquirer.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Judgement. At Mitie, revenue growth produces only modestly faster profit growth, and the mechanism is not pricing power or operating leverage but the arithmetic of a semi-fixed overhead layer plus contracted synergies. EBIT grows at about one and a half to two times the rate of revenue (about 8% a year on 4% to 5% revenue growth), and adjusted EPS grows at about 10% with buybacks. That rate is as good as the business's structure allows.

Evidence and inference, lever by lever

  • Pricing power: none, only pass-through. Mitie recovered 97%, 95% and 94% of wage inflation in FY24 to FY26 and 76% of the FY26 employer National Insurance rise. About 10% of contracts are unindexed, annual price resets lag an April wage rise by up to a year, and change-of-law clauses recover statutory costs only after negotiation. The unrecovered residue is a recurring drag of £10m to £12m a year (15 to 20 basis points), which the cost programmes must earn back before the margin can rise. Real pricing power exists only latently, in compliance (£5m of profit per 1% of real price on about £500m of revenue), and is not in the base case.
  • Operating leverage on volume: low, and rising. About 60% to 65% of costs are front-line labour that transfers with contracts under the Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) regulations, and subcontract and materials spend (over £2bn) follows volume. The incremental EBIT margin on contracted revenue is therefore only about 7% to 10%, against an average margin of 4.7%; Compass's equivalent is about 25%. In margin terms, each 1% of volume adds nearer 5 basis points. Self-delivery, Marlowe's route network (25% drop-through) and the technology layer are raising the fixed share of costs, which helps in the base case but would cost 20 to 30 basis points in a flat-revenue case.
  • Leverage to margin assumptions: high. Because 50 basis points of margin is worth six times as much EBIT as 1% of revenue, cost recovery and synergies matter more than order intake.
  • Financial leverage: low, fixed-rate and unused. Net finance costs peak at about £36m in FY27 (average daily net debt was £523m in Q1 FY27 after Marlowe and the buyback; £360m of notes at 4.65%; lease interest about £10m) and fall by £2m to £3m a year thereafter; rate sensitivity is £1.2m per 50 basis points. Leverage falls from 1.1x to about 0.9x by FY31 after dividends, bolt-on acquisitions and £50m to £75m a year of buybacks, leaving about £100m a year of unused capacity inside the 0.75x to 1.5x target range. The balance sheet therefore helps EPS from FY28, through falling interest and a falling share count, rather than amplifying risk.
  • Cost-out: a treadmill. The cuttable cost layer (central costs of £55m to £60m, divisional overheads, procurement, property and subcontractor mark-ups) is perhaps 8% to 10% of the cost base. A 5% efficiency gain on that layer is £20m to £25m a year, exactly the run-rate Mitie reports, and the inflation residue and client savings claims consume about half of it each year. Peer evidence on automation argues for retention of under half in work priced by headcount: ISS saved 28 million hours and lifted its margin by 40 basis points, while Capita delivered £250m of savings and gave most of them back through 26% to 32% contract price deflation.

Feedback loops: the loops do not compound, and the one self-reinforcing loop runs the wrong way. Two reinforcing loops (scale funds technology, which wins tenders; density and self-delivery capture subcontractor margin) are strongest in FY27 to FY28 and are worth about +50 basis points. Three balancing loops (clients claim automation savings; statutory costs fall outside indexation; delivery failures feed insourcing) are worth about minus 35 basis points now and dominate from FY29. The contract structure converts efficiency into market share and renewals, not margin. The one genuinely self-reinforcing loop runs against Mitie: a visible failure (Capita's pension contract; His Majesty's Prison Millsike) feeds union campaigns and the government's insourcing machinery, which price down re-tenders, which squeeze costs, which raise the chance of the next failure.

So what. No mechanism at Mitie turns 4% revenue growth into 20% profit growth. The only levers that reach shareholders are contracted synergies and an under-geared balance sheet; everything else is passed through to clients or consumed by cost inflation.

Counter-case

Private-equity ownership of OCS and the sector's new discipline could let the two or three remaining national bidders price higher from 2027 (a former Mitie project lead expects exactly that). Compliance could prove to have real pricing power. Marlowe synergies at the Interserve ratio would add 25 to 40 basis points of margin on their own.

What would change the view

Disclosed compliance margins, or compliance price increases held without volume loss; a PRIO savings target with evidence of retention; a Budget shock, which would show how little of the self-help ever reaches shareholders.

Versus the market

Consensus margins (5.0%, 5.3%, 5.4%) show that the market agrees on the path. The market does not articulate the treadmill: about £25m a year of restructuring cash below the adjusted line buys the £20m to £25m of savings that hold the adjusted margin up, so clean EPS runs about 1.5p below adjusted EPS.

Score: 40. No pricing power, low operating leverage on volume, a cost-out programme that mostly offsets inflation and client claims, and balancing loops that cap the margin near 5.5%; the only levers that reach shareholders are contracted synergies and an under-geared balance sheet.

#6Forecast financials: growth, and scope for higher growth and margins than in the past

Judgement. The next four years invert the last six: a revenue-rich, earnings-poor Mitie becomes revenue-modest and earnings-rich. Adjusted EPS compounds at about 10% a year (about 8.5% without buybacks), statutory EPS at over 20% from a depressed base, free cash flow rises from a FY27 trough, and leverage falls below 1x, while reported revenue growth halves as Marlowe annualises. The improvement is real, but half of it is mechanical and already in consensus, and it is modest in absolute terms: 80 basis points of margin over four years.

Versus the market

The model and consensus agree on the operating path to FY29 (EBIT within 1%; revenue within 0.4%). The differences are in composition: buybacks worth 2% to 4% of EPS from FY29 in a break, the share-count basis, the cash definitions, and about £25m a year of restructuring cash that the Analyst treats as an operating cost. #7Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Judgement. There is almost no scope for upgrades while the offer stands, and in a break the first move would be negative. The skew is the wrong way round for an investor hunting upgrades: what the market does not know about Mitie's standalone case is mostly unfavourable, in the window where it would matter.

Evidence and inference

  • Every channel for an upgrade is blocked while the offer stands. Guidance cannot be raised in form (Rule 28 of the Takeover Code); three Hold ratings anchored on the offer pin consensus to the guidance floor; coverage will cease at completion; and the share of Buy ratings is 0% and cannot improve. The Analyst puts the probability of FY27 consensus EPS moving more than 2% before completion at about 30% (20% up on a clean H1, 10% down).
  • In a break, estimates would fall first and rise later. The unfavourable gaps listed below would surface first. The leadership-transition haircut of 3% to 6% to FY28 is smaller than the 10% to 14% cuts that Capita and Green Landscaping suffered when a chief executive left without a successor, because Mitie's succession is already announced. Over the following six to twelve months, upgrades of 2% to 5% would follow from the buyback restart and a clean FY27 print, coverage would widen from three brokers to five or seven, and the share of Buy ratings would jump toward 50% to 70% on valuation grounds. The break-case revision path therefore reads "ratings up, estimates down, then both up".
  • The market narrative is complete on the spread and essentially empty on the standalone mechanisms. The narrative covers the spread and the CMA timetable accurately, with two small arithmetical gaps in the holder's favour: the 1.3p interim dividend is not mentioned, and some retail commentary quotes a spread to 221.6p that double-counts the 3.1p final dividend if that dividend was paid in the normal August window (see the end notes). Nobody states that the margin step is a release of self-help that a new statutory cost step would re-consume; that consensus EPS growth rests on a switch of basis; that £25m a year of restructuring is recurring; that FY26 cash was earned despite a working-capital outflow; which public contracts fall under the Public Interest Test; or that the break-case leadership gap is a succession in progress.
So what. Mitie has no latent upgrade cycle. The one event that can move the price is the CMA decision, and the CMA decision moves the price by closing the spread or breaking the deal, not through estimates.

Counter-case

A clean H1 with "ahead of expectations" wording, plus a benign Budget, could nudge the FY27 margin to 5.1% and FY28 consensus up by 2% to 3%; in a break, those would be the first positive data points for the successor's guidance.

What would change the view

A break. The question would then become the timing of the trough in estimates (likely within a quarter) against the trough in the share price (likely within days).

Versus the market

The Analyst agrees that nothing moves before the CMA decides. The difference is that the Analyst expects the first post-break estimate move to be a cut, where some commentary assumes an immediate standalone upgrade cycle driven by the buyback.

Score: 30. Guidance locked, consensus pinned on the floor, coverage retiring at completion, and a break-case first move that is down; the only upgrades available are small, late and conditional on losing 20% first.

#8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals and peers

Judgement. Mitie's momentum readings describe the offer, not the business. Technical momentum is strong by construction (an uptrend pinned to the offer), sell-side momentum is neutral (estimates drifting up 1% to 2%, no Buy ratings), the narrative is a merger-arbitrage conversation, and the sector's own strong momentum is irrelevant to Mitie while the offer holds the price.

The bid severed Mitie's link with its sector just as that link reached its strongest. In the three months before the bid, Mitie was becoming a sector stock as the sector re-rated: its rolling R-squared against the sector basket had risen to 29% to 33%, with a beta of 0.73 to 0.85, the highest sector linkage in the series. Over the latest six months, the shares have moved idiosyncratically.

  • Guidance momentum: reiterated and locked.
  • Sell-side momentum: three brokers, with a median target price of 219p; the latest estimate date is 9-Sep-2026, and Investec has not touched its model since bid day.
  • Narrative: the discussion is the flow of Form 8.3 disclosures of dealings (LMR Partners, State Street, Norges at 2.2%, Lord Ashcroft) and the CMA case page.
  • Peers: the facility outsourcers re-rated through 2026 on margin delivery, buybacks and de-equitisation (companies leaving the public market). ISS also has B earnings momentum (revision score 12) and has raised its organic growth guidance toward 7%.
So what. Mitie's B technical rating would evaporate on a lapse, because the stock would gap below its 200-day average. The F valuation rating reflects the offer multiple, not a judgement that the business is over-valued. The sector's strength matters only as the anchor for the break-case multiple: 9.5x to 10x, rather than the ten-year median of 9.1x.

Counter-case

The pre-bid data show a stock that had started to trade with ISS and Serco. If the sector's re-rating holds, a broken Mitie would be pulled toward 10x to 10.5x faster than its ten-year history suggests.

What would change the view

A CMA Phase 2 reference (the spread would widen by 5% to 10% even before any break); a sector de-rating led by ISS (which would lower the break-case floor).

Versus the market

There is no disagreement, because the readings are mechanical. The Analyst cautions only against reading the B rating and the 73rd-percentile relative strength as a trend that can be ridden.

Score: 40. Every momentum reading is pinned by a cash bid: a strong tape and a neutral sell-side that cannot upgrade or downgrade, against a sector whose own strong momentum would only matter after a break.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

Judgement. Mitie's risk has two cones that must be kept apart. The financial cone for the next 18 months is narrow for this sector and roughly symmetric; the equity cone is bimodal and wide. The case is simple (two programmes, one calendar, one policy, one regulator), and its fragilities are known and dated. Its drivers are trackable for FY27 but poorly trackable for the items that decide FY28 and the break, and the one risk that is sudden, material and outside the forecasts is a regulator's decision.

The financial cone is narrow because most of the FY27 change is mechanical and most revenue is contracted.

£292m to £312mFY27 EBIT around £304m (minus 4% to plus 3%)
4.9% to 5.2%FY27 EBIT margin
14.4p to 15.8pFY27 EPS, company basis
£130m to £165mFY27 free cash flow, company definition

The skew of the financial cone is slightly positive on FY27 profit (a floor-setter's floor), neutral on FY27 cash and modestly negative on FY28, where the Budget and PRIO retention are the two downside items of size and synergy outperformance is the one upside item. Jefferies' published bracket (a 13.2p bear case with a 4.8% margin and zero organic growth; a 16.8p bull case with 10% organic growth) spans the 5th to 95th percentiles. The cone is narrow for four reasons: most of the FY27 change is mechanical and most revenue is contracted; the half-year print lands before the forecast window is a quarter old; operating leverage on volume is low, so revenue misses become small profit misses; and the balance sheet cannot produce a surprise.

The equity cone is bimodal: about 219.8p with about 90% probability, 160p to 175p with about 10%, and a trough of about 130p in a bad break. The 130p trough is 7.3x earnings, the 10th percentile of the stock's range; Jefferies' stressed value is 115p at 8x on 13.2p. Precedents for lapsed or blocked UK bids show a wide range of outcomes, and Mitie's break case sits in the middle of that range: a strong operating record and balance sheet, offset by a leadership transition, an arbitrage overhang and a market regime that refuses re-ratings to UK mid-caps.

Fragilities and requirements, ranked

  1. The CMA decision: sudden, material and binary, with about a 10% probability of an adverse outcome. Trackable only through the CMA case page.Sudden
  2. The Budget of 28-Oct-2026: dated, with a 15% to 20% chance of a FY26-scale shock costing 20 basis points of FY28 margin. Resolved within days.Dated
  3. PRIO retention: no savings target; peers retained under half of their savings; £10m in the FY28 bridge. Untrackable until management discloses a figure.Untrackable
  4. Marlowe churn: unquantified, with a 25% drop-through, and competitors have withdrawn subcontracted work. Partly trackable through Facilities Compliance revenue at the half year.Partly trackable
  5. Technical Services: minus 5% in Q1, modelled flat for the year; each 3 points of divisional growth is worth £6m of EBIT. Trackable semi-annually.Trackable
  6. The recurring cash cost of other items, and the cash definitions: the company's free cash flow line is a guidance metric, not a modelling line, until the H1 statement reconciles it.H1 statement
  7. Sudden fundamental tails: a failure on a sensitive public contract (prisons, immigration, the Atomic Weapons Establishment, airports, the NHS), costing £10m to £30m plus a political catalyst; an accounting or provisioning surprise (percentage-of-completion projects; £10.8m of dispute provisions; the 2016-2017 history); a cyber attack on operational technology (ISS's 2020 attack cost about DKK 300m).Sudden

Sector and cyclicality: demand is barely cyclical, and Mitie is exposed in substance to only one of the three historical destroyers of UK outsourcers. Demand cyclicality is low: the services are non-discretionary, 90% of contracts are indexed, and Serco held its margins through the 2021-2023 inflation spike. The "false friend" label that an earlier research digest applied to Mitie does not fit the leverage and cash evidence.

Counter-case

Simplicity cuts both ways: with one regulator deciding everything, the holder has no diversification of risk and no information advantage. The CMA's Phase 1 caseload is dropping, but large deals still take nearly double the average time.

What would change the view

A Phase 1 launch with a stated deadline would narrow the equity cone; a Phase 2 reference would widen it sharply; an H1 print confirming the synergy and net-inflation run-rates would narrow the FY27 financial cone further.

Versus the market

The market treats the case as a spread and is right to. The market has not stress-tested the break case in detail, so a break would surprise in its sequence (arbitrage selling first) and in the share count, not in the operating numbers.

Score: 60. One of the simplest and most predictable financial cases in the European sector for 18 months, with low cyclicality and no balance-sheet risk, reduced to the middle of the range by a binary equity outcome that no amount of fundamental analysis can narrow.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Judgement. The dashboard's rule places Mitie at "Turning/Inflecting". The Analyst's view is that the stock's own lifecycle has ended in "acquired": a thesis that broadened (compliance, projects, technology) was bought at the top of its historical valuation range before it could either re-rate on its own merits or stall on growth. If the offer lapses, the stock restarts at "turning up" from a lower base, under new leadership, with its fair multiple set by a sector that has re-rated above Mitie's own history.

◆Dashboard's rule: Turning/Inflecting ■Analyst: acquired; late "thesis broadening", early "stalling on growth" ↗In a break: bottoming, then turning up

Evidence and inference

  • The listed stock's readings are those of a stock whose listed life is being closed out, not one turning up or broadening. Momentum is pinned (technical B by construction; earnings C; estimates +1% to +2%; all ratings Hold). There is no scope for upgrades while the stock is listed, and cuts would come first in a break. The risk factors are one binary regulatory event, a succession, and an approaching policy headwind on public renewals.
  • Read on its own, the standalone business is late in a "thesis broadening" phase and at the start of a "stalling on growth" phase. Reported growth is halving mechanically; organic growth has sat at 4% for three quarters, with leading indicators pointing modestly up; the margin is about to step up after three flat years; the chief executive is retiring; and the plan ends in FY27 with no successor plan. In Richard's framework, that combination of delivery arriving just as the story's architect leaves and growth decelerates is exactly when a stock tends to stall, which is a plausible reason the board took the cash.
  • In a break, the phase would be "bottoming" for about a quarter, then "turning up". Arbitrage selling and consensus cuts would mark the bottoming; the buyback restart, an FY27 margin printed at or above 5% and a successor's FY28 guidance would mark the turn. The break-day price (150p to 165p) would sit below both the break-case fair value (160p to 175p) and the guideline-multiple value at September 2027 (about 189p). The recovery leg would be worth 15% to 25% over 12 to 18 months if the FY27 print is clean and the market regime allows a 9.5x to 10x multiple.
So what. For a listed holder the lifecycle question is moot while the offer stands. For Richard's framework, a break would create a reversion setup, not an upgrade setup: "cause for concern clearing in a medium-quality, low-cyclicality business on a Q1 multiple, leading to reversion to normal". The concerns that would need to clear are the lapse itself, the succession and the Public Interest Test, and "normal" would be a multiple of 9.5x to 10x.

Counter-case

The dashboard's "Turning/Inflecting" label is defensible for the standalone business: order intake is up 33%, renewals are at 91%, and a margin step is arriving after three flat years. Ignoring the bid, the fundamentals are inflecting up.

What would change the view

Only a lapse, which would make the phase question live again; the identity and tone of the successor chief executive would then matter most.

Versus the market

The market does not think about Mitie's lifecycle phase at all; it thinks about the CMA. The Analyst agrees that the CMA is the right focus now, and adds that the phase analysis is what a non-holder should prepare for the day the CMA focus stops being right.

Score: 45. A thesis bought before it could stall or re-rate: the standalone business is inflecting up on margin and down on growth as its architect leaves, and only a bid lapse would reopen a lifecycle that could then read "bottoming, then turning up".

#11The fair multiple

Judgement. The guideline fair multiple of 9.52x two-year-forward earnings (the 60th percentile of Mitie's ten-year range, the guideline for the Turning/Inflecting phase) is the right centre for the break case. The Analyst would put a range of 9x to 10.5x around it, leaning to 9.5x to 10x: 9x for a bad break with a long succession, 10.5x for a clean break with the buyback restarted and the sector holding its 2026 re-rating. While the offer stands, the multiple is 12.0x to 12.6x by construction, and no fair-multiple view changes it.

Evidence and inference

  • Mitie's own history. The five-year median is 9.3x, within a range of 6.5x to 12.4x. Today's multiple is 12.0x on the dashboard (the 95th percentile) or 12.6x on the model's EPS. The stock traded at 8.3x to 9.6x through 2024, at 10x to 11x through most of the pre-bid 2025-2026 period as the sector re-rated, at 8.8x at the June 2026 low (149p), and at 12x since the bid.
  • Why the break-case centre should sit above the ten-year median. The sector re-rated in 2026 (ISS 11.8x, at the 63rd percentile of its own history; Serco 11.7x; Sodexo 13.6x; Elis 9.8x), Mitie's pre-bid beta to the sector was about 0.8, and the business has an above-median record of delivery, high returns on capital and leverage of about 1x.
  • Why the centre should sit below the two closest peers (11.7x to 11.8x). Mitie has a chief executive succession in progress; UK public exposure of 45% to 50% meeting the Public Interest Test; a 106% gap between adjusted and statutory earnings that narrows only from FY28; arbitrage selling on a break; a market regime that refuses re-ratings to UK mid-caps; and thin broker coverage.
  • What the offer multiple says. The 218.5p offer is 15.1x consensus FY27 EPS of 14.5p (15.4x on Deutsche Bank's numbers), 14.4x the model's FY27 EPS, about 12x two-year-forward EPS, and about 8.5x FY27 EBITDA including leases, on an enterprise value of about £3.45bn. Listed UK outsourcers trade at about 9x EBITDA while private buyers pay 12x, so the price can be both the top of Mitie's own range and no more than fair against private deals.
  • Phase sensitivity. In a peak-delivery phase (clean FY27 print, buyback running, successor credible), 10.2x (the 75th percentile) would be defensible; in a stalling phase (Budget shock, Technical Services leaking revenue, public insourcing visible), 8.5x (the 35th percentile) is the conservative reading. The guideline's 9.52x splits the two sensibly.
So what. On brokers'-basis 24-month-forward EPS of about 17.5p, each turn of the multiple is worth 17.5p of value: 9x gives 158p, 9.52x gives 167p, 10x gives 175p and 10.5x gives 184p.

Counter-case

A lapsed bid can leave a stock below its undisturbed price for a long time (Hammerson, Renishaw). Mitie's undisturbed price was 151p (8.8x), after a 16.6% fall in the three months before the bid, and the market regime (US ten-year yields of about 5.1%; UK mid-caps out of favour) argues for the low end of the range.

What would change the view

Lower: ISS and Serco de-rating. Higher: a clean FY27 print under a named successor with the buyback running. A counter-bid would make the question academic again.

Versus the market

The market's multiple is 12x because a bidder is paying it. Brokers' pre-bid targets implied 10x EV/EBIT (Deutsche Bank, 195p) and 12x FY27 EPS (Jefferies, 170p). The Analyst accepts the guideline as the centre and leans a little above the ten-year median, for the sector reason.

Score: 22. The current multiple is a cash price at the 95th percentile of the stock's history, with the guideline fair multiple 21% below it, so the fair-multiple gap is unfavourable; the guideline itself is sound and, in a break, would sit modestly below where the two closest listed peers trade.

#12Total shareholder return

Judgement. Mitie offers two separate returns, which must be presented separately. The completion case returns about 4.3% in four to five months (about 11% annualised), with no earnings, multiple or dividend component beyond the 1.3p interim dividend. The break case is the model's return at the guideline fair multiple: minus 10.4% to 30-Sep-2027 and plus 6.4% to 31-Mar-2029 (2.6% a year), because a 25% to 26% de-rating from 12.6x to 9.52x outweighs 16% to 33% of earnings growth and 2% to 8% of dividends. Weighted by probability, the expected value of a holding bought at 210.8p is about 212p to 214p, which is the risk-free rate.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple (break-case path, from 211p on 22-Oct-2026)

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedValue (p)DividendsMultipleEarnings
To 30-Sep-2027 (the 18-month column)minus 10.4%minus 11.1%189+2.4%minus 25.0%+16.2%
To 31-Mar-2029 (the three-year column)+6.4%+2.6%224+7.9%minus 26.0%+33.1%

What drives the break-case return

  • The multiple does the damage. The fall from 12.6x to 9.52x is a 24.4% de-rating, which the template reports as minus 25% and minus 26% once the earnings base shifts. The de-rating is the removal of the bid premium, expressed as a multiple.
  • Earnings do the work. Earnings growth of +16% over 18 months and +33% over three years is adjusted EPS compounding at about 10% to 11% a year from the 13.6p FY26 base (15.2p in FY27, 17.0p in FY28 and 18.6p in FY29 on the Analyst's share count; the model's share-count convention gives about 2% less by FY30).
    Where the three-year EPS growth comes from
    Margin step 4.7% to 5.4%: about 40%
    Volume: about 30%
    Interest: 15%
    Buybacks: 15%
    Volume at a 7% to 10% incremental margin; interest falling; share count falling from FY28 buybacks.
  • Dividends add 2.4% and 7.9%. Dividends of 5.0p, 5.6p and 6.1p for FY27 to FY29 are a third of adjusted EPS, a yield of about 2.4% rising to 2.9% on today's price.
  • Arithmetic check. 1.162 × 0.75 × 1.024 = 0.892 (minus 10.8%); 1.331 × 0.74 × 1.079 = 1.063 (plus 6.3%). The three-year return turns positive only because three years of earnings growth outrun a one-off de-rating.
How to read the model's return. The model's path starts from today's pinned price and asks what happens if the pin is removed and the stock settles at the guideline multiple. The path is therefore the break-case return for a holder who neither sells on the break nor is bought out; it is not the completion case. It also understates the break case's volatility: the stock would not glide to 189p by September 2027 but would gap to 150p to 165p first and then recover. From a break-day price of 155p, the same 189p is a 22% gain in eleven months, which is the "reversion to normal" leg described in #10.

The completion case: 4.3% now, then cash to redeploy. If the CMA runs to the long-stop of 21-Jul-2027, the annualised return falls to about 6%. If the 3.1p final dividend has not in fact been paid, the receipt is 3.1p higher and the spread is 5.7% (see the end notes).

The probability-weighted view over the next 6 to 18 months: about the risk-free rate, with a fat left tail. 90% × 219.8p plus 10% × about 165p (the break-case value after the first quarter of selling and re-rating) gives about 214p; discounting the cash leg at 4% for four and a half months gives about 212p. Against 210.8p, the expected return is 0.5% to 1.5%. Over three years, the completion case returns cash (so the return depends on how the cash is redeployed), and the break case returns the model's +6.4%.

Counter-case

If the deal breaks and the sector holds its re-rating, the break-case multiple could be 10x to 10.5x rather than 9.52x, lifting the 18-month value to 198p to 208p and the return to minus 6% to minus 1%. A counter-bid, however unlikely, would produce a return above the spread.

What would change the view

A Phase 2 reference (the probability-weighted value would fall toward 200p); a Phase 1 clearance (the spread would close to about 1% to 2% at once); any change to the completion timetable, which changes the annualised return on the spread more than the absolute return.

Versus the market

The market prices exactly this outcome: a fair spread. The Analyst adds only that the model's negative 18-month return at the guideline multiple describes the break-case path, not a prediction of loss, and that the break-day overshoot would be the moment at which the standalone case offers a positive expected return.

Score: 30. A fairly priced 4.3% spread with a one-in-ten chance of a 20% to 25% loss gives an expected return close to cash over the next six months, and the break-case path at the guideline multiple is negative over 18 months because a 25% de-rating outweighs 16% of earnings growth.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Mitie is a well-run, asset-light, cash-generative leader of a structurally low-margin industry, and its owners have sold it at the top of its own valuation range. The sale price sits in the middle of the private-market range, and the sale comes four months before Mitie was due to deliver the margin step it had promised for three years.

The standalone case is sound and unusually predictable for 18 months. Mitie will very probably meet the FY27 margin floor of 5%, because for the first time since FY24 the annual self-help is not being spent absorbing a statutory cost shock. The FY28 step to about 5.3% rests on contracted Marlowe synergies and one benign Budget.

Beyond FY28, the industry's structure caps the story. Mitie has no pricing power, its efficiency gains go to clients, its public book meets the Public Interest Test from FY29, and its margin ceiling is near 5.5%. The earnings base is the weakest foundation (a 106% gap between adjusted and statutory EPS; about £25m a year of restructuring that is an operating cost in substance), the cash is better than its reputation, and the management record is excellent and departing.

For a listed holder, none of the standalone analysis is the investment case. The case is a 4.3% spread to about 219.8p, resolved by one regulator over the next three to five months, against a 9% to 11% chance of a lapse. A lapse would take the price to 150p to 165p on the day, and to a fair value of 160p to 175p once arbitrage selling, consensus cuts, a buyback restart and a succession had played out. The price has that one-in-ten chance right: the spread pays the risk-free rate for the tail. There is no upgrade cycle to be found, because guidance is locked, consensus sits on the floor and the first move after a break would be down. The one moment at which Richard's framework could apply is a break-day price below 160p, which would set up a reversion to the guideline multiple (about 189p by September 2027) in a medium-quality, low-cyclicality business under new leadership; that setup is one to prepare for, not one to pay for now.

What to watch, in order

  1. The CMA case page: Phase 1 launch, deadline and decision
  2. Autumn Budget, 28-Oct-2026: the April 2027 wage floor and any employer cost step
  3. H1 FY27 results, 19-Nov-2026: an H1 margin of about 4.5%, synergies of about £6m, Facilities Compliance revenue, the wording of the £150m cash guidance, and any PRIO savings number
  4. Interim dividend record date, 27-Nov-2026
  5. Court timetable, calendar Q1 2027

End notes

Bases of the figures. Figures are on the company's basis unless stated. Operating profit is before other items and is called "EBIT" throughout; "other items" are the costs the company excludes from adjusted profit. EPS is adjusted, basic and on the company's basis (FY26 13.6p) unless marked "brokers' basis" (FY26 12.6p, diluted). The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 2 (the "forecasts of record"). Money is in pounds sterling.

The two EPS share-count conventions. The model's EPS (0.15, 0.17, 0.18, 0.20 and 0.22 pounds in its own rounding) retires buyback shares at the model's own price convention. The Analyst's EPS of 15.2p to 22.3p assumes break-case buyback prices of 160p to 190p, which gives about 2% more EPS by FY30.

The 3.1p final dividend. The memo could not verify whether the 3.1p FY26 final dividend was paid in the normal August window. Some retail commentary quotes a spread to 221.6p, which double-counts that dividend if it was paid. The payment date should be checked before acting: if the dividend has not been paid, the expected receipt is 3.1p higher and the spread is 5.7%.

Sources of the visuals. The default charts and tables use FactSet history (reported basis) and consensus (FactSet median, brokers' basis), the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model (update 2) and the Master Dashboard's price, relative strength and valuation charts. The drawn charts and text visuals (the payoff tree, approvals, timeline, judgements chart, cost calendar, synergy bars, moat tiles, peer bars, guidance record, FY27 EBIT bridge, EPS bases, margin attribution, cost-programme record, scenarios, two cones, break-case sequence, offer-multiple comparison, value per multiple, return cards and EPS growth sources) take their figures from the memo's text. Where history (FactSet) and the model differ in basis, for example FY26 EBIT of £200m in FactSet's table against £264m on the company's basis, the memo's text uses the company's basis.

Names used. CMA: Competition and Markets Authority. CD&R: Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, owner of OCS Group. DWP: Department for Work and Pensions. PRIO: Mitie's agentic artificial intelligence programme. Viewforth: the house forecasts (the Financial Analyst's model). Rule 28: the profit-forecast rule of the UK Takeover Code.
